title: The True Tabernacle and the New Covenant
summary: The main point is this: believers have a high priest seated at God's right hand who serves in the true sanctuary in heaven, of which the earthly tabernacle was a copy and shadow. His ministry is superior because the covenant he mediates is better, founded on better promises. The author quotes Jeremiah's prophecy of a new covenant, written on hearts, with universal knowledge of God and full forgiveness, and concludes that by calling it new God has made the first covenant obsolete.
story: Chapter 7 established that Jesus is a priest in the order of Melchizedek. Chapter 8 opens the next stage of the argument, which runs to 10:18: where this priest serves and under what covenant. The author announces his main point in verse 1, then introduces two themes that he will develop in the following chapters, the heavenly sanctuary (chapter 9) and the new covenant (chapters 9-10). The new covenant was not a Christian invention. It was promised by Jeremiah centuries earlier, in the dark days before the Babylonians destroyed Jerusalem. Hebrews reads that promise as fulfilled in Jesus.
historical:
Jeremiah prophesied in Judah in the late seventh and early sixth centuries BC, through the final decades of the kingdom and the destruction of Jerusalem and its temple by the Babylonians in 587 or 586 BC. His promise of a new covenant (Jeremiah 31:31-34) came in a section of the book often called the Book of Consolation (chapters 30-33), which looks beyond judgment to restoration. Its quotation here in verses 8-12 is the longest quotation of the Old Testament in the New.

The covenant made at Sinai (Exodus 19-24) is what Hebrews calls the first covenant. Its priesthood and sacrifices were tied to the tabernacle, the portable tent-sanctuary Israel carried in the wilderness, built according to the pattern God showed Moses on the mountain (Exodus 25:40, quoted in verse 5). The Dead Sea community at Qumran also spoke of a new covenant and saw itself as the faithful remnant with whom God had renewed it, which shows that the hope of Jeremiah 31 was alive among Jews in the period.
cultural:
Many ancient peoples believed that earthly temples copied heavenly ones, where the gods truly dwelt. Israel's Scriptures shared a version of this idea: Moses was shown a pattern, and the tabernacle was built to match it. The language of copy and shadow in verse 5 also resembles the vocabulary of Plato, who taught that visible things are imperfect copies of eternal ideal forms, and Philo of Alexandria combined Platonic language with Jewish interpretation. Scholars debate how much Hebrews draws on this philosophical background and how much on Jewish apocalyptic writings, which describe a real heavenly temple. Hebrews seems to use both vocabularies, but its thinking is historical as well as spatial: the shadow comes first in time, and the reality arrives with Christ.

A covenant in the ancient world was a binding relationship with promises and obligations, often sealed by oath and sacrifice. The formula "I will be their God, and they will be My people" was the heart of Israel's covenant with God throughout the Old Testament.
literary: The chapter has two parts. Verses 1-6 state the main point and set up contrasts between heaven and earth, true and copy, better and inferior ministry. Verses 7-13 frame the quotation of Jeremiah 31:31-34 with the author's comments: if the first covenant had been faultless, no second would have been sought (verse 7), and by calling it new God has made the first old (verse 13). Note that the author says God "found fault with the people" (verse 8); the problem with the old covenant was not the law's holiness but the people's failure to keep it. Jeremiah's prophecy has four promises: God's law written on hearts, a restored relationship, knowledge of God for all, and forgiveness of sins. The last promise, "I will forgive their iniquities and will remember their sins no more", will be quoted again in 10:17 to close the whole argument.

outline.t: The main point: a high priest in the true tabernacle
The earthly copy and the better ministry
Jeremiah's promise of a new covenant

doctrines.note: God's covenant purposes run through the whole Bible. The new covenant fulfills the old covenant's aim, that God would be the God of a people who truly know and obey him, by writing his law on hearts and forgiving sins completely.

In the new covenant God's laws are not abolished but internalized: "I will put My laws in their minds and inscribe them on their hearts." What was external and often broken becomes a matter of transformed desire.
The new covenant's final promise, the forgiveness of sins remembered no more, requires a sacrifice that truly deals with sin. Chapters 9 and 10 will show that Christ's sacrifice is that foundation.

words.note: Diatheke, covenant, used five times in this chapter. In ordinary Greek it could mean a last will or testament, and the author will play on that meaning in 9:16-17. In the Greek Old Testament it translates the Hebrew berit, God's binding covenant relationship with his people.

Skia, shadow. A shadow is real but insubstantial, and it points to the object that casts it. The earthly tabernacle and its priesthood are a shadow of heavenly realities (verse 5); in 10:1 the law is a shadow of the good things to come.

Tupos, pattern, model, or impression. Moses built according to the tupos shown him on the mountain (Exodus 25:40). The English word type, used for Old Testament patterns that point to Christ, comes from this word.

Kainos, new, often in the sense of new in quality rather than merely recent. The new covenant is not just a later edition of the old but a fresh kind of relationship, with the law written on the heart and sins forgiven.

christ: Jesus is the high priest who "sat down at the right hand of the throne of the Majesty in heaven" and serves in the true tabernacle that God himself set up. He is also the mediator of the new covenant, the one through whom God's promise to Jeremiah comes true. The Gospels record that at the Last Supper Jesus spoke of the cup as the new covenant in his blood (Luke 22:20; see also 1 Corinthians 11:25), consciously taking up Jeremiah's promise. The forgiveness, heart-renewal, and knowledge of God that the prophet longed for become available through him.

hard.q: If the first covenant is "obsolete", what does that say about the Jewish people and Judaism?
hard.a:
The chapter's language has sometimes been used to support contempt for Jews, and Christians have a long and shameful history of such contempt. It is important to read the text carefully. The author is himself steeped in Israel's Scriptures and speaks of the old covenant as God's own work. He quotes a Jewish prophet promising a new covenant "with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah". His point is that God himself announced something new, and that the old covenant's priesthood and sacrifices pointed forward to it.

Christians hold different views on how this relates to the Jewish people today. Some hold that the church has replaced Israel as God's people (sometimes called supersession or replacement theology). Others, including many who draw on Romans 9-11, hold that God's calling of Israel remains, that the new covenant was promised first to Israel, and that the Jewish people still have a place in God's purposes, even as Christians confess Jesus as the one Messiah for Jew and Gentile alike. Since the Holocaust, many churches have repudiated teachings that fed hostility toward Jews. Hebrews concerns the fulfillment of God's promises in Christ, not the condemnation of a people.

questions: The new covenant promises that God's law will be written on hearts. What is the difference between obeying a rule from outside and wanting what God wants?
The author says the old tabernacle was a copy and shadow of something greater. What good things in your life point beyond themselves to something more?
The final promise of the new covenant is forgiveness: God will remember sins no more. How might truly believing that change the way you carry your past?
